passage:
I'm Sunaina. Relief came first, Vikas. I remember sitting on my hostel bed after saying to myself, for the first time, that I don't believe in God. My chest felt lighter, like putting down a bag I'd carried since childhood.

Then the loneliness arrived. At Diwali I stood in the kitchen while my mother and aunts sang, and I didn't know where I fit.

For a while I was a little proud of being the rational one. I rolled my eyes at things. Then my grandmother caught me at it and asked quietly, "Does it hurt you if I pray?" It didn't. That stopped me.

Now I try to say what I actually live by: telling the truth, showing up for people. I go to the puja for my family and sit through it respectfully.

qa.q: Where was Sunaina sitting when the relief came?
qa.a: Sunaina was sitting on the hostel bed.

qa.q: What did Sunaina feel after the relief, and what shows it?
qa.a: Loneliness: at Diwali Sunaina stood in the kitchen while the others sang and didn't know where to fit.

qa.q: What did the grandmother's question help change?
qa.a: It stopped the eye-rolling pride, and now Sunaina names values like telling the truth and showing up for people while respecting believers by sitting through the puja.

qa.q: How might the grandmother feel about the eye-rolling?
qa.a: The grandmother may feel a little hurt or curious, but asks quietly rather than scolding, which suggests she wants to understand.

grounding: Sunaina settles into being an atheist, feels relief and some loneliness, and chooses named values and respect for believers over pride.

passage:
'So you're saying it officially now? Atheist?' Pooja asked, passing the chips.
'I think so,' Chinmay said. 'Agnostic, maybe. I just don't believe any of it the way I used to.'
'How does it feel?'
'Lighter. Honestly. Like I stopped pretending in my own head.' He paused. 'And a bit lonely. Everyone at home is doing Ganpati this week.'
'Are you going?'
'Yes. Aai would be so hurt if I didn't. And I like the modaks and the drumming. It's family.'
'Didn't you say rituals are just superstition last month?'
Chinmay winced. 'I did. I was being a smart-aleck. I felt clever for about a day.' He picked at the chips. 'I don't want to be that person. I want to be someone who's honest, keeps promises, is kind to Aai. Those I can name.'
'That's a better list than a lot of people have,' Pooja said.
'Don't say that at my house,' he laughed.

qa.q: What festival is everyone at home celebrating this week?
qa.a: Everyone at home is celebrating Ganpati.

qa.q: How does Chinmay feel about calling himself an atheist?
qa.a: Chinmay feels lighter and relieved, but also a bit lonely with family celebrating.

qa.q: What values does Chinmay choose to live by?
qa.a: Being honest, keeping promises and being kind to Aai, while still joining the family's festival.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay's Aai be hurt if he skipped Ganpati?
qa.a: For her it is family and faith together, so his absence might feel like rejection.

grounding: Shows settling into non-belief with relief and some loneliness, choosing named values, and respecting the family's rituals instead of mocking them.

passage: I'm Dolma, and in my second year I decided I didn't believe in rebirth or anything else my grandmother taught me. It felt like taking off a heavy coat. I was relieved. I was also, if I'm honest, a little proud of myself, as if I had seen through something nobody else could. One evening in the hostel, Charu was keeping a fast for her fiancé, and I laughed and said, 'You know the moon doesn't care, right?' She didn't answer. Later I heard her on the phone, voice small, telling her mother she felt stupid. That stopped me. I had called myself rational and then been cruel. I knocked on her door and apologised. Now I try to live by things I can name: be truthful, don't harm, help when I can. I still light a butter lamp with my grandmother when I'm home, for her. I'm lonelier than I was. But I'm less proud, and kinder.

qa.q: What did Dolma say to Charu about the fast?
qa.a: Dolma said, 'You know the moon doesn't care, right?'

qa.q: How did Dolma feel after deciding not to believe?
qa.a: Dolma felt relieved, like taking off a heavy coat, and a little proud.

qa.q: What did Dolma learn to do instead of mocking?
qa.a: To apologise, respect Charu's practice, and live by named values like truthfulness and not harming.

qa.q: How did Charu feel after Dolma's remark?
qa.a: Charu felt small and stupid, telling her mother so on the phone.

grounding: A first-person account of settling into non-belief with relief and loneliness, catching the pride of being 'rational', and choosing respect and named values.
